newsitem.title: UK: Sterling skids to below $1.61 and 3.03 marks.
newsitem.headline: Sterling skids to below $1.61 and 3.03 marks.

text.p: Sterling stumbled to near five-month lows below $1.61 and lost some three-pfennigs to below 3.03 marks in nervous dealings ahead of the outcome of the Bank of England's monetary policy committee meeting, said traders.

An initial bout of profit-taking on cable, sparked by U.S. and Asian names, pushed the pair through stops around key support of $1.62 - dragging sterling/mark in its wake. Dealers said a powering dollar/mark, which scaled to near eight-year peaks highs of 1.8876, weighed on an already shaky cable.
The BoE, whose two-day meeting starts Wednesday, is due to announce its decision on interest rates at 1100 GMT on Thursday.

At 0845 GMT, cable was trading at $1.6050/60 against $1.6262/72 in late Europe on Tuesday. It was off lows around $1.6005 hit in early dealings. Sterling/mark was at 3.0255/65 against 3.0545/56 in late Europe, though off lows around 3.0203 marks hit earlier.
A Reuter poll said 16 out of 23 economists surveyed expected rates to rise from their current level of 6.75 percent to 7.0 percent - the fourth-quarter point increase since May.
But traders said sentiment was mixed and the market was nervous as the risks grew of steady rates after the BoE's meeting ends on Thursday.
"Once sterling went throught he $1.62 area it hit stops...People are perhaps hedging their bets for no-change in the BoE's monetary policy committee," said Peter Wood, trader at Bank of Boston.
"People are getting panicky and jumping on the bandwagon while it is moving," said Wood.

Traders said there is mounting concern as the general strength of sterling, which scaled to 3.0878 marks and its highest since August 1989 in late July, chokes off exports and threatens unemployment. Sterling's trade-weighed index stood at 104.5 compared to its close of 105.7 on Tuesday.
"The market is getting very nervous and is starting to take profits (at these levels)," said Lee Ferridge, currency strategist at Commerzbank.
Rising interest rates and the persistent strength of sterling are putting London's economic boom in jeopardy, the London Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI) said on Wednesday.

An LCCI survey showed that 55 percent of service sector companies reported that high interest rates were the biggest threat to economic prosperity, whilst amongst manufacturers, interest rate rises are second only to high exchange rates on the list of worries.
